title: P99/P95 tail latency deep dive - Aegis Systems
next_steps: Share benchmark spreadsheet and raw trace logs
Run 2-hour p99 load test with 1k RPS using our p95/p99 harness
Provision VPC private deployment trial for Aegis staging (1 node, 2 vGPU)
Send SOC 2 + network diagram + KMS/HSM integration doc
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-06-23
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~75 minutes
Attendees (Redwood): Jordan Meyers (AE), Priya Kapoor (SE), Luca Chen (SRE)
Attendees (Aegis): Marta Ruiz (CTO), Daniel Park (Platform Engineer), Sofia Gomez (ML Engineer)

Auto-generated summary (may be rough):
Aegis is evaluating Redwood for latency-sensitive inference. Primary concerns: p95/p99 tail latency for short/medium prompts, streaming vs non-streaming behavior, network hops when using VPC/private deployment, KV cache hit rates and how batching/quantization affects tail. They want an initial 2-hour benchmark and a private VPC trial. Action: Redwood to share benchmarks, run tests, and send security docs.

Topics: p95/p99 tail, KV cache behavior, batching trade-offs, quantization impact, streaming vs non-streaming, network hops and cross-AZ variance, private VPC deployment, next steps (benchmarks + trial)

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Meyers: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Um, we, we wanted to run through the p95/p99 tail latency stuff you mentioned in the questionnaire. 
[00:10] Marta Ruiz: Yep, thanks Jordan. We, we saw some spikes in prod last week. p95 is okay but p99 is blowing out to 900–1,200ms which is—yeah—too high for our realtime flows.
[00:22] Priya Kapoor: Got it. Can you give us a quick sense of the workload? tokens per request, sequence lengths, streaming or non-streaming?
[00:30] Daniel Park: Mostly short prompts, 30–60 tokens, but we do some multi-turn where the KV gets longer, up to maybe 800 tokens in the context. We stream in the UI, but the backend also does non-streaming batch inference for async tasks.
[00:45] Sofia Gomez: Also, we're on a multi-AZ GCP setup, some requests cross zones because of our routing. Not sure if that's contributing.
[00:52] Luca Chen: yeah crossing AZs will add 10–30ms typically, and then egress cost but—um—more importantly you'll see jitter.
[01:05] Jordan Meyers: Ok let's break down sources: model compute, batching delays, KV cache misses, network hops, and serialization/ingress. Priya, do you want to walk through the runtime behavior?
[01:15] Priya Kapoor: Sure. On the runtime side, the big contributors to tail are: (1) cold KV cache — when prefix/key not hot, we have to rehydrate; (2) batching waiting window — if we enlarge the batching window to improve throughput you'll increase tail; (3) kernel scheduling and fallback quant paths — certain quantized kernels can take a bit longer for short sequences due to kernel startup. Also streaming has different path: streaming yields tokens as they compute; non-streaming waits for full completion so observed tail can look worse or better depending on how you measure p99.
[01:50] Marta Ruiz: Wait, quantization — we currently run 8-bit INT8 on a custom build. Does that often add tail?
[01:58] Priya Kapoor: It can. Quantization reduces compute per token but some int8/x4 fused kernels have a higher variance for short sequences due to, uh, kernel launch and memory format conversions. For bulk long sequences it's great; short prompts sometimes see slight headroom loss, which shows up in p99.
[02:15] Daniel Park: Hmm, interesting. What about the KV cache? We saw some calls where subsequent turns are fast but the first is slow.
[02:22] Priya Kapoor: That's classic. If your application doesn't use prefix caching or the model variant doesn't share KV layout, you'll re-fill the KV cache which adds a nonlinear penalty. Also network RPC to your cache store (if external) will add variability.
[02:35] Sofia Gomez: Our cache is internal to the serving node but we do have occasional evictions set aggressively.
[02:41] Luca Chen: Evictions are a big one — and also if your KV gets spilled to disk or remote NFS it'll kill tail. We usually recommend keeping KV in GPU memory, and for Aegis scale you have to size the cache and tune TTL.
[02:58] Jordan Meyers: okay let's talk numbers. What p95/p99 are you seeing in different scenarios? Marta?
[03:05] Marta Ruiz: For our realtime stream: p95 ~230ms p99 ~1100ms. For non-streamed batch: p95 ~450ms p99 ~1300ms. Under a burst test we saw p99 jump to 2.3s.
[03:20] Priya Kapoor: From Redwood side, with our typical 13B open models on a dedicated GPU pool, for 40–60 token prompts we usually target p95 < 150ms and p99 < 400ms on optimized kernel profiles and hot KV. But across networked VPCs and cross-AZ you'll add 30–100ms depending on topology.
[03:38] Daniel Park: The cross-AZ number aligns. Some of our spikes coincided with backup jobs that saturated NICs. So it'd be helpful to isolate network hops.
[03:48] Priya Kapoor: For that we suggest: enable per-request tracing (we can provide tracing hooks from Redwood Console), and run a synthetic benchmark that pins clients to same AZ and different AZ to quantify delta. We have a benchmark harness that reports p50/p95/p99 plus token-by-token latency traces.
[04:05] Sofia Gomez: Can you explain more about streaming vs non-streaming? Our UX gets partial tokens then stitches them. But we see bigger p99 in streaming sometimes which is counterintuitive.
[04:15] Priya Kapoor: Yeah, streaming surfaces the earliest token latencies; if a request has a high-to-low distribution of compute across tokens you'll see that the initial tokens might be quick but later tokens delayed; also the metric semantics differ — are you measuring time to first token, or to last? Streaming often shows lower time-to-first-token but higher time-to-final if there are taily kernels or cache misses mid-run. Also if you measure p99 of time-to-first-token you'll miss last-token tails.
[04:45] Jordan Meyers: Another important piece is batching strategy. We do continuous batching with a short delay window. If you set the max batch size high, throughput increases but p99 spikes because some requests wait. If you set max latency low, then throughput drops. We can tune per-route.
[05:00] Marta Ruiz: We want high throughput for background tasks but low tail for user-facing requests. So maybe route them differently?
[05:06] Priya Kapoor: Exactly — route user-facing to low-latency pools with smaller batching windows and hot KV; background to high-throughput pools with larger batches and possibly higher quantization. Redwood supports routing policies: latency-first vs cost-first.
[05:20] Daniel Park: About VPC/private deployment: if we deploy Redwood Private VPC inside our GCP project, are there additional network hops when the control plane talks to the runtime?
[05:30] Luca Chen: If you choose Private with customer-managed VPC, the data plane remains in your network; control plane calls are minimal and can be proxied. The thing to watch is cross-subnet or cross-AZ routing. Also ensure MTU and jumbo frames aren't causing fragmentation — that slips by many teams.
[05:45] Sofia Gomez: And KMS/HSM for keys — any impact on tail?
[05:49] Priya Kapoor: KMS calls are typically done at session start or token refresh; not per-request. If you do per-request signing it's a problem. We support local caching of DEKs to avoid per-request KMS latency. We'll send the KMS integration guide.
[06:05] Marta Ruiz: We saw p99 spikes during autoscaling events. Any best practices?
[06:10] Luca Chen: Autoscaling can add variance. Warm pools, pre-warm model instances, and use graceful rollouts. Also prefer horizontal scale with sticky routing rather than spin-up cold instances. For dedicated pools we can reserve burst capacity.
[06:25] Jordan Meyers: We'll propose a test plan: replicate your prod-ish routing pattern, run short/long sequences, measure p50/p95/p99 and token latency distribution, vary quantization (fp16 vs int8), and test streaming vs non-streaming.
[06:40] Marta Ruiz: Sounds good. Can we dig into an example trace? We captured a flamegraph where a single request spent 320ms in 'KV fetch' and 180ms in scheduling.
[06:52] Priya Kapoor: Can you upload that? But yes, if KV fetch is 320ms that's frequently the issue — either remote KV store, eviction, or pack/unpack between host and device. We recommend keeping KV resident on GPU or using a fast on-node cache; if you must remote-store, ensure it's co-located and has low latency (RDMA or local NVMe).
[07:10] Daniel Park: Our KV store is sharded across nodes and uses a sidecar over gRPC. Could that be the culprit?
[07:16] Luca Chen: Sidecars add serialization and queueing. gRPC is ok but configure keepalives and increase concurrency. Also inspect threadpool saturation on the node.
[07:28] Sofia Gomez: For quantization tests, what numbers should we expect?
[07:32] Priya Kapoor: For a 13B family model, fp16 p95 ~120–150ms p99 ~350–450ms (hot KV). For int8 you might see p95 drop to 80–110ms but p99 could remain similar or in some cases increase if kernel variance is high. For very short sequences, benefit sometimes small.
[07:52] Marta Ruiz: Hmm so int8 maybe risky for user-facing flows unless we verify p99.
[07:58] Jordan Meyers: Right — common pattern: use int8 for background batch jobs, use fp16 for realtime. Or tune fast kernels and fused ops for the int8 path.
[08:06] Daniel Park: On the network side, you said cross-AZ can be 30–100ms. Our users require 200ms p99 SLA. If base compute is 150ms, we only have 50ms headroom. That's tight.
[08:18] Priya Kapoor: Then you'd want co-located runtimes in the same AZ and route users to nearest AZ. Also ensure you use private network (VPC) instead of public internet. For critical flows, Redwood Dedicated in your VPC with pinned nodes will help.
[08:33] Marta Ruiz: Does Redwood support per-route kernel profiles? Like smaller batch windows for certain endpoints?
[08:39] Priya Kapoor: Yes — per-route configs. You can set max-latency-ms, target batch size, cache TTL, quantization profile, and failover policies.
[08:50] Jordan Meyers: Let's go through the planned benchmark: 1) baseline: fp16, no quant, warm KV, same-AZ clients at 1k RPS for 2 hours; 2) int8 profile same test; 3) cross-AZ variant; 4) streaming vs non-streaming measure time-to-first and time-to-last token. We'll collect per-token traces and histograms.
[09:10] Marta Ruiz: We'll also run with realistic traffic: 90% short prompts, 10% long context.
[09:15] Priya Kapoor: Great. We'll also instrument deeper traces: GPU kernel timings, scheduler latency, and network RTTs. We'll send the harness and the config.
[09:26] Daniel Park: About logs and compliance — will logs include PII? We need to ensure we can disable transcript storage and have audit logs only.
[09:33] Priya Kapoor: Yes — you can opt out of transcript retention and enable redaction. For Private deployments logs stay in your project. We'll include SOC 2 and logging controls in the packet.
[09:45] Marta Ruiz: One concern: our model code does some custom tokenizers and a preprocessor. Does that sit in the critical path?
[09:52] Luca Chen: If preprocessor runs in the same request path it will add variability. Best practice: do lightweight preprocess on the client or a dedicated preprocessing service with predictable scaling.
[10:03] Jordan Meyers: Quick detour — anyone using function/ tools calls? That can also add external latency.
[10:09] Sofia Gomez: We call a vector re-ranker in the pipeline occasionally. That is another external hop.
[10:14] Priya Kapoor: Right — every external RPC multiplies tail. Where possible consolidate into same node or async them.
[10:21] Marta Ruiz: For the initial trial, we'd like to test on our staging cluster with a Private deployment. What's the typical turnaround?
[10:27] Jordan Meyers: We can stand up a 1-node trial in your VPC within 3–5 business days once networking details are done. We'll need an infra contact for peering or shared VPC details.
[10:37] Marta Ruiz: That'll be Daniel.
[10:39] Daniel Park: yep. I can share VPC CIDRs and a small list of ports.
[10:43] Priya Kapoor: We'll also provide a checklist: MTU, subnet routing, CPU pinning, NIC offload settings, and driver versions.
[10:51] Sofia Gomez: Can you show an example of the tracing output?
[10:55] Priya Kapoor: Sure, I'll paste an example in the follow-up email — the harness output includes per-token latencies, which we can visualize and show where the tail originates.
[11:05] Jordan Meyers: Let's address some common mitigations quickly: 1) Keep KV hot — increase cache size and reduce eviction; 2) Use low-latency pooling for user routes; 3) Route background to high-batch compute with quantization; 4) Co-locate runtimes in same AZ and avoid cross-AZ traffic; 5) Pre-warm instances before rollout; 6) Measure both time-to-first and time-to-last token for streaming.
[11:28] Marta Ruiz: Sounds actionable. A few Qs — can you demo how batching window changes p99?
[11:34] Priya Kapoor: Yes, we can spin a short demo. But better to run it on your staging data so it's realistic.
[11:40] Daniel Park: For the benchmark harness, what client load tool do you use?
[11:44] Priya Kapoor: We use a custom harness built on wrk with token-level tracing, plus k6 for scenario scripting. We'll share the repo.
[11:52] Sofia Gomez: Any gotchas for GPU drivers and quantized kernels?
[11:56] Luca Chen: Make sure CUDA, cuDNN, and driver versions match recommended builds. Some quant kernels are sensitive to driver versions and may fallback to slower paths if incompatible. Also ensure NUMA and memory interleaving are tuned.
[12:10] Marta Ruiz: Are there any quick wins we can do in the next week?
[12:13] Priya Kapoor: Short-term: pin user routes to low-latency pool, increase KV memory eviction threshold, instrument per-request traces, and avoid cross-AZ routing for critical flows. We'll send the specific commands.
[12:25] Jordan Meyers: Okay let's capture the concrete next steps now.
[12:28] Marta Ruiz: sure.
[12:30] Jordan Meyers: Next steps summary (from Redwood): 1) Share benchmark harness + instructions (item: Priya), 2) Run 2-hour p99 load test with 1k RPS in staging and share traces (item: Aegis/Daniel + Redwood), 3) Provision Private VPC trial (item: Jordan + Daniel), 4) Send SOC2 + KMS + network checklist (item: Jordan), 5) Schedule a follow-up to review results (item: all) — propose next week.
[12:53] Daniel Park: I'll provision a small staging subnet and run the baseline next Tuesday.
[12:58] Marta Ruiz: Can you also include the per-route config example for small-batch user endpoints?
[13:03] Priya Kapoor: Yes, example config will be in the follow-up.
[13:08] Sofia Gomez: One last thing — what about degradations: if p99 spikes, can we auto-fallback to a smaller model to reduce latency?
[13:14] Priya Kapoor: Yes, Redwood supports automatic fallback policies: you can define a cheaper/lower-latency variant as a fallback when tail or CPU/GPU utilization crosses thresholds. It helps maintain availability.
[13:25] Jordan Meyers: Great. Any final Qs?
[13:28] Marta Ruiz: No, thank you — that was super helpful.
[13:31] Jordan Meyers: Thanks everyone. We'll drop the harness and the SOC2 packet by EOD tomorrow.
[13:36] End meeting.

Recap (verbatim-ish):
- Primary issue: p99 tail spikes to ~1.1s in streaming and ~1.3s in non-streaming for short prompts, with cross-AZ/network and KV eviction contributing.
- Planned tests: 2-hour p99/p95 run at 1k RPS, fp16 vs int8, same-AZ vs cross-AZ, streaming time-to-first vs time-to-last token.
- Mitigations: keep KV hot, per-route low-latency pools, pre-warm, co-locate runtimes, use fallback models, tune batching windows.

Explicit next steps (copied):
- Share benchmark spreadsheet and raw trace logs (Jordan/Priya)
- Run 2-hour p99 load test with 1k RPS using our harness (Aegis + Redwood)
- Provision VPC private deployment trial (Jordan + Daniel)
- Send SOC 2 + network diagram + KMS/HSM integration doc (Jordan)

References mentioned: Redwood Console tracing, benchmark harness repo (link forthcoming), SOC2 packet (link forthcoming), per-route config examples (link forthcoming).

Notes on transcription: Some speaker labels may be approximate and a few technical terms may be mis-transcribed (e.g., "K-V cash" instead of KV cache).
